On a turn, someone rolls two six-sided dice. Each player then writes the results, e.g. 1 and 4, in empty spaces in the pattern, with each number being in the mirrored space of the other. After all spaces are filled, you calculate the score. Each 1 on its own — that is, with no other 1s orthogonally adjacent — scores 1 point; each set of two 2s that have no other orthogonally adjacent 2s score 2 points; and so on up to a set of six 6s. Whoever has the highest score wins. Number of players: 1 - 12 Game duration: 8 mn Complexity: 0 / 5 Play Splitter and 1414 other games online. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary IDEA OF THE GAME Every round, all players write down the same number (1–6) on their score sheets, but (usually) in different positions. After 22 rounds, each player will have completely filled in their score sheet. If at the end of the game, exactly two 2‘s are directly adjacent to each other, you score 2 points. If exactly three 3’s are directly adjacent, you score 3 points. For exactly four adjacent 4‘s, you score 4 points, and so on. The two star spaces double the points you score there. HOW TO PLAY Each player receives an identical score sheet. (For your first game, we recommend using game pad A. You can find the rules for game pad B and the solo variant at the end of this rulebook.) Two dice are rolled. All players must write both numbers on their sheets. Each player may freely choose where to write the numbers, but there is one rule they must follow: • Both numbers must be symmetrical to the center line: they must be written down in the same row, at an equal distance from the center. You may choose which number you want to write down on the left, and which on the right. Once all players are finished, both dice are rolled, all players write down both numbers again. Repeat until all spaces are filled on the scoresheet. SCORING Points are calculated as follows: • 1 POINT For each 1 that‘s on its own, meaning there are no other 1’s orthogonally adjacent to it (diagonally is allowed). •2 POINTS If exactly two 2’s are orthogonally adjacent. If more than two 2's are touching, score nothing for them. •3 POINTS If exactly three 3’s are orthogonally adjacent. •4 POINTS If exactly four 4’s are orthogonally adjacent •5 POINTS If exactly five 5’s are orthogonally adjacent •6 POINTS If exactly six 6’s are orthogonally adjacent Numbers that are diagonally next to each other are not considered adjacent. Score for each separate group of the same number. For example, if you manage to create three separate groups containing exactly three 3‘s, you score 3 points per group. STAR SPACES double the value of a valid group. The player with the highest final score wins. If there‘s a tie, those players share the victory. GAME PAD B The play area on game pad B also contains 44 spaces, 2 of which are star spaces. The same rules as in the normal game apply: there are no changes. However, the three heart spaces are new, which means the following rules are added: • Numbers are written down in the three heart spaces according to the normal rules. If at the end of the game you managed to write down the same number in all three heart spaces, you score 5 bonus points. Note: it doesn‘t matter whether these numbers are part of a valid group or not SOLO PLAY The rules and scoring do not change when playing a solo game. You can use either side of the scoresheet (Game Pad B allows you to score an extra 5 points, but the rows are shorter, making it slightly more difficult). Compare your final score to this list to see how you did: 27 points or less: you lose 28-30 points: welcome to the club 31-33 points: okay 34-36 points: decent 37-38 points: nice 39-40 points: great 41-42 points: top notch 43-44 points: world class 45-46 points: amazing 47-48 points: spectacular 49-50 points: unbelievable 51 points or more: otherworldly Board Game Arena would like to thank Nürnberger-Spielkarten-Verlag f

[Rating: 1/10] I don't like roll and writes (and cannot fathom the craze) and this shitty game does nothing to change my mind. I guess if you enjoy rolling dice you might like it. Like a worse version of Minesweeper (and I'm not even a fan of that game). There are literally hundreds and hundreds of great games. If you are bored there are great solo games. Or you can read a book.

[Rating: 2/10] Maybe a harsh rating but it's just not very fun. Reminds me of On Tour a bit - a roll and write where you are filling in based on probabilities and hope, and then you get screwed by dice and end up with another score that is the same as your last five. Points for simplicity I suppose.

[Rating: 3/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  Solo activity that many people can play at the same time. More of a puzzle than a game really but using dice and trying to set up groups dependent upon the number. Meh.

[Rating: 3/10] Rather basic roll-and-write game. I have a hard time seeing people get excited about this, whether solo or multiplayer. It seems odd that barring special features each scoring group has the same points-to-squares ratio, even though larger groups are obviously harder and riskier to set up.

[Rating: 3/10] What I like: - The Trickster's Table app successfully tricked me into playing a roll and write. - Something to dabble around while sitting in the metro. Inoffensive and puzzly. Very easy rules.  What I dislike: - Multiplayer solitaire. - Only played the solo variant but comparing the scores of various plays makes little sense since the dice rolls will always be different. - Last few turns can turn pretty frustrating if only the wrong dice values come up. I'm not a big dice player connoisseur but I usually like it when there's a least some ways to influence/change the dice.

[Rating: 4/10] If this had pre-dated Qwixx it might have stood out, but I think the ground is now pretty well-trod.  [1 play]

[Rating: 4/10] It’s biggest draw is you can play it anytime, anywhere and teach anyone… the game itself is a bit too simple
